items.name: Readability
items.evidence: The code was only inline one-liners with single-letter names in business logic: `d=open(...)`, `c=sqlite3.connect(...)`, `r=[{"id":i,"name":n,"value":v ...}]`. There are no comments and no named script. The intent is clear only because the code is so short.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: There is no re-runnable decrypt or extract script, only `python3 -c` one-liners mixed with shell commands. It is short and leaves no scratch files, but it can't be reused and does not split decrypt and extract into separate units, as the project conventions ask.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: `b^0x42` is a hardcoded key in the code; it is only justified in the final message. Nothing checks the WAL magic after decrypting, there is no error handling, and the connection is never explicitly closed. No errors are swallowed, though.

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: The key came from the header ("first 4 bytes, XORed with 0x42424242, give ... 0x377f0682"). The agent decrypted the whole file, let SQLite replay the WAL via `sqlite3.connect` and `select ... order by id`, and checked the count (`print(r,len(r))` -> 11). It did not run integrity_check.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: `cp main.db-wal /tmp/wal.bak && cp main.db /tmp/main.db.bak` ran before the in-place overwrite and before any SQLite open. That mattered: SQLite later checkpointed and deleted the WAL.
